title: The Configurations Database — Overview: the shape of a system
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. A configuration is the set of choices that makes a generic system into a specific one: which services start, which ports open, which defaults rule. Configurations live in files, registries, firmware menus, and cloud services, and they are the usual suspect when something breaks — the code is innocent, the config is guilty. This database records configurations as first-class records: what was set, why, and how to reproduce it. Reproducible configuration is the difference between a system and a snowflake.
capabilities: Configuration as the choices that specialize a system
Configs live in files, registries, firmware, cloud
The usual suspect: config guilty until proven innocent
Reproducible configuration vs snowflake systems

title: The Configurations Database — Operating system configuration
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Operating systems are configured in layers: Windows keeps settings in the registry and group policy; macOS uses plist files and profiles; Linux scatters text files across /etc — sshd_config, fstab, sysctl.conf — each with its own syntax and its own way to break booting. Package managers, services, users, and firewall rules complete the picture. The professional habit is scripted configuration: every change as code or command history, so a fresh machine can be rebuilt identically. The demo parses classic key=value config lines.
capabilities: Windows registry and group policy
macOS plists and configuration profiles
Linux /etc: sshd_config, fstab, sysctl.conf
Scripted configuration: rebuild any machine identically

title: The Configurations Database — BIOS and UEFI setup
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Before the operating system loads, firmware decides: the boot order chooses which disk or network boots first; Secure Boot verifies signatures on bootloaders against platform keys; the TPM stores measurements and secrets for disk encryption; fan curves trade noise for cooling; virtualization extensions (VT-x, AMD-V) must be enabled for virtual machines to run fast. Firmware settings are the foundation — misconfigure them and no OS configuration can compensate. The demo validates a boot order list.
capabilities: Boot order: which device boots first
Secure Boot and platform key verification
TPM for measured boot and disk encryption
Fan curves and virtualization extensions

title: The Configurations Database — Network device configuration
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Routers and switches are configured as text: interfaces get addresses, VLANs segment traffic, ACLs permit or deny, routing protocols (OSPF, BGP) exchange reachability. The golden rules are backup before change, change in maintenance windows, and keep the last-known-good config one command away. Configuration management tools push identical configs to fleets of devices and audit drift. The demo validates VLAN IDs against the legal range.
capabilities: Interface addresses, VLANs, ACLs, routing protocols
Backup before change; last-known-good one command away
Fleet-wide config push and drift auditing
Maintenance windows for network changes

title: The Configurations Database — Application setup profiles
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Applications keep their own configurations: dotfiles (.bashrc, .vimrc, .gitconfig) carry a developer's personality between machines; browsers sync profiles; editors export settings as JSON. The professional pattern is a dotfiles repository — version-controlled, symlinked into place by a setup script — so a new laptop becomes home in minutes. Profiles separate concerns: work and personal, each with its own extensions, bookmarks, and secrets. The demo deep-merges a default profile with user overrides.
capabilities: Dotfiles: carrying personality between machines
Version-controlled setup scripts for new machines
Profiles that separate work from personal
Defaults merged with user overrides

demo.title: Deep merge profiles
demo.code: function merge(a,b){const o={...a};for(const k in b)o[k]=(typeof b[k]==='object'&&typeof o[k]==='object')?merge(o[k],b[k]):b[k];return o;}const m=merge({theme:'dark',font:{size:12}}, {font:{size:14}});J(m);assert(m.theme==='dark'&&m.font.size===14,'merge');

title: The Configurations Database — Containers and infrastructure as code
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Modern infrastructure is configuration all the way down: Dockerfiles declare how images are built, compose files declare how services wire together, and Kubernetes manifests declare desired state — deployments, services, config maps — for the cluster to enforce. The discipline is declarative: describe what should exist, let the tooling converge reality to the description, and keep every description in version control. Secrets stay out of manifests, injected at runtime. The demo substitutes environment variables into a config template.
capabilities: Dockerfiles, compose files, Kubernetes manifests
Declarative: describe desired state, converge reality
Everything in version control
Secrets injected at runtime, never in manifests

title: The Configurations Database — Feature flags and configuration services
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Feature flags separate deployment from release: code ships dark, then a flag flips it on for a percentage of users, a region, or a plan tier. Kill switches roll back in seconds without redeploying. Configuration services (and simple config files) centralize the flags so every instance reads the same truth. The discipline is flag hygiene: every flag has an owner and an expiry, because forgotten flags become permanent branches. The demo evaluates a percentage rollout deterministically.
capabilities: Separating deployment from release
Percentage rollouts and kill switches
Centralized flags: one truth for all instances
Flag hygiene: owners and expiries

title: The Configurations Database — Configuration backup and recovery
body: Public edition. Sourced public knowledge, fact-checked reference; never mixed with Signature records. Configurations are backed up because rebuilding from memory is how outages are born. Version control holds every config file with commit messages explaining why; automated snapshots capture device configs nightly; restore is tested, not assumed — an untested backup is a rumor. Disaster recovery plans name the order: restore network, then identity, then data, then applications, verifying each layer before the next. The demo diffs two config snapshots and lists what changed.
capabilities: Version control for every config file
Nightly automated snapshots of device configs
Restore tested, never assumed
Recovery order: network, identity, data, applications

demo.title: Config diff
demo.code: function diff(a,b){const changed=[];for(const k of new Set([...Object.keys(a),...Object.keys(b)]))if(a[k]!==b[k])changed.push(k);return changed;}const d=diff({p:80,h:'a'},{p:8080,h:'a',t:1});J({changed:d});assert(d.length===2&&d.includes('p'),'cfgdiff');
